summary: Given an array and a target, return the indices of two distinct elements whose values sum to the target (exactly one answer exists).
mainInsight: For each x the partner you need is target - x. A hash map from value to index turns 'has the partner appeared earlier?' into an O(1) lookup, so a single pass is enough.
invariant: Before processing index i, the map holds every value at indices < i (value -> index), and no valid pair using only indices < i has been missed.

approaches.name: Brute force
approaches.summary: Check every pair (i, j) with i < j.
approaches.interviewRelevance: Always state it first as the baseline, then optimise.

approaches.name: Sort + two pointers
approaches.summary: Sort (value, original index) pairs, then move two pointers inward from both ends comparing the sum with the target.
strengths: Becomes O(1) extra space if the input is already sorted
weaknesses: Sorting loses original indices, so you must carry them along
approaches.interviewRelevance: Good follow-up: 'what if the array is sorted?' (Two Sum II).

approaches.name: One-pass hash map
approaches.summary: Iterate once; if target - x is already in the map return both indices, otherwise store x -> i.

commonMistakes: Inserting the current number before checking its complement (reuses the same element, e.g. [3,2,4] target 6).
Sorting the array and forgetting the original indices.
edgeCases: The two elements are adjacent / at the extremes.

promptVariants: What is the key pattern behind the optimal Two Sum solution?
Which technique gives the standard one-pass solution for Two Sum?
What interview pattern should you recognise for Two Sum?
cards.explanation: The hash map stores previously seen values so each complement lookup is O(1) on average.

incorrectOptionExplanations.Sliding window: There is no contiguous-window constraint; the two elements can be anywhere.
incorrectOptionExplanations.Binary search: It needs sorted data; sorting would destroy the original indices you must return.
incorrectOptionExplanations.Monotonic stack: There is no nearest-greater / nearest-smaller structure in the problem.

promptVariants: Why does using a hash map eliminate the need to check every pair?
What does the hash map buy you compared with brute force?
Explain the core idea of the O(n) Two Sum solution.
cards.answer: For each element x the only partner that works is target - x. Instead of scanning for it (O(n) per element), the map answers 'have I seen target - x?' in O(1), so n lookups replace n^2 pair checks.
keyPoints: Partner is fully determined: target - x
cards.explanation: Brute force is n scans of length n. A hash map precomputes 'what I have seen' so each scan collapses to one lookup.

promptVariants: What information should the hash map contain at iteration i?
State the loop invariant of the one-pass solution.
At index i, what do the map's keys and values represent?
cards.answer: Keys are the values at indices 0..i-1 and each maps to its index. Therefore if a valid pair ends at i, its earlier element is in the map.
keyPoints: Guarantees any earlier partner is findable
cards.explanation: Because the current element is inserted only after the check, the map never contains index i itself while we look for its complement.

promptVariants: Why should the complement be checked before inserting the current number?
What goes wrong if you insert nums[i] into the map before the lookup?
Why is the order 'check, then insert' important?
options: The same element could be paired with itself
The map would no longer be sorted
Dictionary lookups only work on keys not yet inserted
cards.answer: The same element could be paired with itself
cards.explanation: If x is inserted first and 2*x == target, the lookup finds x itself and returns [i, i], reusing one element.

incorrectOptionExplanations.The map would no longer be sorted: Hash maps are unordered; order is irrelevant here.
incorrectOptionExplanations.Dictionary lookups only work on keys not: Lookups work on any existing key; this is not a dictionary restriction.
incorrectOptionExplanations.It halves the memory usage: The memory use is identical either way.

promptVariants: Time complexity of the one-pass hash-map solution: ___
The optimal Two Sum solution runs in ___ time (average case).
cards.explanation: One pass of n elements, each doing an O(1) average-time dictionary lookup and insertion.

promptVariants: Space complexity of the one-pass hash-map solution: ___
In the worst case the map stores up to n entries, so extra space is ___.
cards.explanation: In the worst case (no pair until the end) every element is stored in the map.

promptVariants: What is the time-space trade-off between brute force and the hash-map solution?
How do brute force and the hash-map approach compare on time and space?
options: Hash map: O(n) time / O(n) space vs brute force: O(n^2) time / O(1) space
Hash map: O(n log n) time / O(1) space vs brute force: O(n^2) time / O(n) space
Hash map: O(n) time / O(1) space vs brute force: O(n^2) time / O(n) space
Both are O(n^2) time; the hash map only saves constant factors
cards.answer: Hash map: O(n) time / O(n) space vs brute force: O(n^2) time / O(1) space
cards.explanation: You spend O(n) memory on the map to remove the inner loop: a classic time-for-space trade.

incorrectOptionExplanations.Hash map: O(n log n) time / O(1) space v: That mixes up the approaches; O(n log n) belongs to sorting and the hash map is not O(1) space.
incorrectOptionExplanations.Hash map: O(n) time / O(1) space vs brut: The map needs O(n) space; brute force needs none.
incorrectOptionExplanations.Both are O(n^2) time; the hash map only: It removes the entire inner loop: n^2 -> n.

promptVariants: Why does the one-pass solution still work when duplicate values exist (e.g. [1,6,6,2], target 12)?
Trace [1,6,6,2] with target 12 through the hash-map solution. Why is the duplicate not a problem?
cards.answer: At index 0 the complement 11 is not in the map, so 1 -> 0 is stored. At index 1 the complement 6 is not in the map yet, so 6 -> 1 is stored. At index 2 the complement 6 IS in the map (index 1), so we return [1,2] before the second 6 could overwrite the entry.
keyPoints: Overwrite of duplicate keys never matters because the answer is returned first
cards.explanation: Overwriting a key only loses the older index, which only matters if a later element needed it - but a valid pair would already have been returned.

promptVariants: Why is 'sort then two pointers' not the preferred Two Sum solution?
What is the main drawback of sorting first in Two Sum?
options: Sorting costs O(n log n) and loses the original indices
Two pointers cannot find sums in an already sorted array
Sorting makes duplicate values impossible to handle at all
It needs O(n^2) memory to track all of the pairs
cards.answer: Sorting costs O(n log n) and loses the original indices
cards.explanation: You must return original indices, so you have to carry (value, index) pairs through the sort, and the sort makes it O(n log n) instead of O(n).

incorrectOptionExplanations.Two pointers cannot find sums in an alre: Two pointers works on sorted data (it is the Two Sum II solution).
incorrectOptionExplanations.It needs O(n^2) memory to track all of t: Memory is O(n) for the index pairs.

promptVariants: What breaks if `seen[x] = i` is moved above the `if need in seen` check?
Swap the insert and the lookup below. For which input does the answer become wrong?
cards.answer: When 2*x == target the lookup finds x's own entry, returning [i, i] (e.g. nums=[3,2,4], target=6 returns [0,0]) - the same element is used twice.
cards.explanation: Insert-after-check guarantees the map only contains earlier indices.

promptVariants: If the array were already sorted and you must use O(1) extra space, what would you do?
How would you solve Two Sum on a sorted array without a hash map?
cards.answer: Use two pointers, lo = 0 and hi = n-1. If the sum is too small move lo right; if too large move hi left; stop when it equals the target. O(n) time, O(1) space.
keyPoints: Sum too small => lo++, too large => hi--
cards.explanation: Sortedness gives monotonic information: moving lo increases the sum, moving hi decreases it.
